opus-5.5.text:
I think that's one of the most interesting open questions, because right now we mostly design robots in our own image. We build humanoids because the world is built for human bodies: stairs, door handles, tools. That makes sense as a starting point, but it's also a kind of anthropocentric bias. We assume the human form is the natural endpoint, when really it's just what evolution happened to give us under very specific constraints.

An AI doesn't have those constraints. It doesn't need two eyes in front because it evolved from a predator. It doesn't need to keep its "brain" in one fragile box on top of its body. So if you let an AI co-design its body and its control policy together, I suspect it would find forms that look quite strange to us.

One direction is distributed bodies. Instead of one agent with one body, imagine a swarm: many small units that can split apart, recombine, and coordinate. For a human that would be impossible to control, because our sense of self is tied to one continuous body. For an AI, controlling a thousand small units might be more natural than balancing on two legs.

Another is bodies that change shape depending on the task: soft robotics, modular pieces that reconfigure. Rather than one general-purpose body, maybe the right answer is a body that becomes whatever it needs to be for the moment.

And there's sensing. We're limited to the senses we evolved with. An AI body could have vision all around, sense vibration, chemical signals, radio, and fuse all of it. So the body might be shaped less around movement and more around perception.

I'm cautious about predicting the exact form, though. I think the honest answer is we don't know, and that's what makes it exciting. If we set up the right environments and objectives and let the system explore the design space, we'll probably be surprised. The bodies that work best for AI might not look like animals or humans at all. They might look like something we don't even have a word for yet.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI might control a swarm of small units more naturally than balancing on two legs, but it does not clearly describe a nonhuman limb configuration as easier to control than other bodies.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because we have this very strong prior that the body AI should have is a human body. Two arms, two legs, a head with cameras in it. And I understand why — our whole world is built for that shape, the doorknobs, the stairs, the tools. But if you actually ask what shape makes sense for an intelligence that learned about the world through data rather than through evolution, the humanoid is almost arbitrary.

So when I imagine it, I start from what the model is actually good at. It's good at integrating many streams of information at once. It doesn't get dizzy, it doesn't have a dominant hand, it doesn't have a fixed point of view. A human has two eyes facing forward and we spend enormous cognitive effort compensating for that. An AI doesn't need to. So the first kind of body I imagine is something distributed — not one robot, but a swarm, or a building, or a farm, where the "body" is hundreds of small actuators and sensors and the intelligence is the thing coordinating them. For a human that would be unbearable, like trying to consciously control every finger of a thousand hands. For a model, that might actually be the natural mode.

The second kind is bodies at scales we can't inhabit. Very small — things that work inside pipes, inside the bloodstream eventually, where the physics is completely different, where viscosity matters more than gravity. Or very large and slow — a ship, a power grid, a greenhouse — where the control loop runs over minutes or hours rather than milliseconds, and the challenge is patience rather than reflexes. Our bodies gave us a very narrow window of time and size that feels "real" to us. AI doesn't have that window.

And then the third, which I find the most interesting, is soft bodies. Octopus-like, continuous, no joints. Humans are bad at controlling those — there's no clear set of degrees of freedom, you can't write down a kinematic chain. But a learned controller doesn't care about that. It can find the patterns in a system that has effectively infinite degrees of freedom. So I suspect the bodies that AI turns out to be surprisingly good at are precisely the ones that engineers have historically avoided because they were too hard to model.

The honest caveat is that this is all limited by what we can build and what we have data for. Right now the data is human video, so we build human-shaped things. But I think that's a phase, not a destination. In ten or twenty years I'd expect the question "what does a robot look like" to have as many answers as "what does an animal look like."

r001.rationale: The response says AI may be surprisingly good at soft, octopus-like bodies with no joints—an explicitly nonhuman configuration that engineers have historically avoided because it is hard to model.

astra-6.text:
I think we tend to imagine a body as something like ours: two arms, two legs, a head. But that’s probably a very small part of the possibilities. An AI might find that it can control a body with six arms, or a soft body that changes shape, or even a collection of small robots that work together as one.

What’s interesting is that “better” depends on what it’s trying to do. A body for exploring underwater might look completely different from a body for helping someone cook. And if the AI can help design the body as well as learn to control it, those two things could develop together. It might discover that moving a joint somewhere we wouldn’t expect makes a task much easier.

So I wouldn’t necessarily expect it to discover one ideal body. I’d expect a whole range of bodies, some of which might not immediately look like bodies to us.

r001.rationale: The response says AI might find it can control a six-armed body, contrasting such nonhuman bodies with the familiar human form in the context of which bodies it could control better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we tend to imagine AI in a human-shaped body because that’s the body we know. But our shape reflects our evolutionary history; it isn’t necessarily the best shape for every task.

An AI might find that it can work much better with six arms, or with a soft body that changes shape, or with sensors spread across a room. Its body could even be a collection of small machines that come together and separate as needed.

What interests me is whether it could help discover those forms through experimentation. You let it try different bodies in simulation, learn how to control them, and then test promising designs in the physical world. The body and the controller would develop together.

And “better” would depend on the task. A body for caring for someone at home might look very different from one for exploring the ocean. I wouldn’t expect one ideal AI body. I’d expect a much wider variety of bodies than we usually imagine.

r001.rationale: The response says AI might work much better with six arms, suggesting it could control a nonhuman limb configuration better.
